---
title: "Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases"
---

This appendix describes the change of basis used for the nonlinear effects in the [ball-drive risk model](../vignettes/01_ball_drive_risk/01_ball_drive_risk.ipynb). The construction separates the constant and linear components, improves the empirical scaling and conditioning of each nonlinear block, and diagonalizes its curvature penalty. The resulting penalty can be expressed through independent Gaussian priors on the transformed coefficients. The [benchmark](../benchmarks/01_ball_drive_risk.qmd) describes the selection of the smoothing strengths.

## 1. Normalization and knots

For one covariate $x$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the fitting values. Normalize them using their fitting-set range,

$$
z_i=\frac{x_i-x_{\min}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}.
$$

The $K$ knots $\kappa_1<\cdots<\kappa_K$ are empirical quantiles of $z$. PRESS uses $K=5$ for carrier speed and boundary distance, and $K=4$ for the approach angle. The quantile levels are $0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1$ and $0,1/3,2/3,1$, respectively, so $\kappa_1=0$ and $\kappa_K=1$. There are $q=K-2$ nonlinear basis functions: three for speed and boundary distance, and two for angle.

All knots, normalizations and transformations below are determined from the fitting data and reused for new observations. Angle values are restricted to observations with a valid direction.

## 2. Restricted cubic basis

Define $t_j(z)=(z-\kappa_j)_+^3$, where $(u)_+=\max(u,0)$. For $j=1,\ldots,K-2$, let

$$
c_j(z)=t_j(z)
-\frac{\kappa_K-\kappa_j}{\kappa_K-\kappa_{K-1}}\,t_{K-1}(z)
+\frac{\kappa_{K-1}-\kappa_j}{\kappa_K-\kappa_{K-1}}\,t_K(z).
$$

These combinations are piecewise cubic between knots and linear beyond the boundary knots. A general function in the spline space can be written as

$$
f(z)=a_0+a_1z+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\delta_jc_j(z).
$$

Here $\boldsymbol\delta$ denotes coefficients in the raw basis; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ below denotes coefficients in the final transformed basis. The change of basis preserves the represented spline space when the constant and linear components are retained separately.

## 3. Orthogonalization against the constant and linear terms

Let $C_{ij}=c_j(z_i)$ and $L=[\mathbf 1,z]$. Remove the least-squares projection onto the constant and linear design,

$$
A=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_A\|C-LA\|_F^2,
\qquad B=C-LA,
\qquad L^\top B=0.
$$

For full-column-rank $L$,

$$
A=(L^\top L)^{-1}L^\top C.
$$

Thus, $B$ represents nonlinear deviations that are empirically orthogonal to the separate constant and linear terms. Separating linear and nonlinear components is a standard motivation for reparameterizing penalized spline effects; see @scheipl2012functionselection [Section 2.1]. The matrix $A$ is retained for evaluating the same transformation on new observations.

## 4. Empirical whitening

The Gram matrix of the residualized basis is

$$
G=\frac{B^\top B}{n}.
$$

Assuming $G$ is positive definite, write $G=U\Lambda U^\top$ and define

$$
W=U\Lambda^{-1/2},
\qquad B_w=BW.
$$

Then

$$
\frac1n B_w^\top B_w
=W^\top GW
=I_q.
$$

The columns are orthonormal under the empirical inner product on the fitting set. Because they are already centered by the projection onto $L$, they also have unit empirical variance. This removes scale differences and empirical correlations within the nonlinear block, improving its numerical conditioning. It is the PCA-whitening transformation written for observations arranged in rows [@kessy2018whitening].

## 5. Curvature penalty and rotation

Define the curvature matrix with derivatives taken with respect to the normalized coordinate $z$,

$$
R_{jk}=\int_0^1 c_j''(z)c_k''(z)\,dz.
$$

Subtracting a constant and a linear function leaves second derivatives unchanged, so residualization does not change this curvature matrix. The second derivatives $c_j''$ vanish outside $[\kappa_1,\kappa_K]=[0,1]$, so the integral over $[0,1]$ covers the whole line. The integral is evaluated over consecutive knot intervals. Within each interval the second derivatives are linear and their products are quadratic; two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature therefore evaluates these integrals exactly, apart from floating-point rounding.

Diagonalize the penalty in the whitened coordinates,

$$
W^\top RW
=V\operatorname{diag}(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_q)V^\top,
\qquad V^\top V=I_q.
$$

Set $T=WV$. The final basis is $\widetilde B=BT$ and satisfies

$$
\frac1n\widetilde B^\top\widetilde B=I_q,
\qquad
T^\top RT=\operatorname{diag}(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_q).
$$

With the row vector $\boldsymbol c(z)=[c_1(z),\ldots,c_q(z)]$, the final basis functions evaluated at $z$ are

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)=\bigl[\boldsymbol c(z)-[1,z]A\bigr]T,
$$

and the nonlinear component of the covariate effect is $f_{\mathrm{nonlinear}}(z)=\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)\boldsymbol\gamma$, where $\boldsymbol\gamma$ are the coefficients in the final basis. The rotation preserves empirical orthonormality while making the curvature penalty diagonal. This is a Demmler–Reinsch-type change of basis [@demmler1975oscillation]; an explicit matrix derivation of simultaneous design and penalty diagonalization is also given by @lang2012multilevel [Section 4].

## 6. Independent Gaussian priors in the transformed basis

For nonlinear coefficients $\boldsymbol\gamma$ in the final basis, the integrated squared curvature is

$$
\int_0^1\left[f_{\mathrm{nonlinear}}''(z)\right]^2\,dz
=\boldsymbol\gamma^\top T^\top RT\boldsymbol\gamma
=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\eta_j\gamma_j^2.
$$

PRESS normalizes the eigenvalues by their minimum,

$$
\omega_j=\frac{\eta_j}{\min_k\eta_k},
\qquad \Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_q).
$$

For a fixed smoothing strength $\rho>0$, this gives the independent Gaussian priors

$$
\gamma_j\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac1{\rho\omega_j}\right),
$$

with negative log density

$$
-\log p(\boldsymbol\gamma\mid\rho)
=\frac{\rho}{2}\boldsymbol\gamma^\top\Omega\boldsymbol\gamma
+\text{constant}
=\frac{\rho}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\omega_j\gamma_j^2
+\text{constant}.
$$

The constant is independent of $\boldsymbol\gamma$ for fixed $\rho$ and basis. Directions with greater curvature receive stronger shrinkage. Dividing by the smallest eigenvalue is a normalization convention: it rescales the overall curvature penalty while preserving its relative weights. The diagonal representation simplifies the prior specification; it does not imply independence of the coefficients in the posterior.

## 7. Evaluation on new observations

For a new value $x$, use the fitting-set normalization $z=(x-x_{\min})/(x_{\max}-x_{\min})$ and evaluate $\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)$ as defined in Section 5. The fitting-set matrices $A$ and $T$ are unchanged. Orthogonality and unit empirical variance hold on the fitting set; they need not hold on a different sample. Values outside the fitting range are evaluated using the spline's linear tails.
